articles.title_orig: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians and Washington Post photographer in West Bank
articles.title_zh: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians and Washington Post photographer in West Bank
articles.content_orig:
Photojournalist Heidi Levine leaves a hospital emergency room in a wheelchair in the Israeli-occupied city of Ramallah, West Bank. She's being treated after an attack by Israeli settlers as she was photographing Palestinian farmers harvesting their olives, in the Palestinian village of Abu Falah on Friday. Ahmad Gharabli/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians as they were harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank on Friday, injuring several people including an American photojournalist.
The Washington Post said photographer Heidi Levine was reporting in the West Bank, wearing a protective vest clearly marked as "press," when she was beaten.
"Today I was brutally attacked," Levine said in a video filmed at a hospital and posted online ."We saw in the distance, in the hilltop, I would say at least 50 masked men, slingshots. And when they came running down, I was attacked, pushed to the ground," she said, "they just kept kicking me and kicking me." They also stole her cameras and phone.
She said medical workers rushed her in an ambulance to a hospital. Washington Post Executive Editor Matt Murray said in a statement the paper was relieved that Levine received medical care and is safe, but denounced the violence against her.
"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," Murray said.
The Post said the attack happened when Palestinians were trying to harvest their olives. It said settlers set Palestinian olive groves on fire and hurled stones using slingshots.
Israeli soldiers move toward a Palestinian man lying wounded on a road after they shot him following a settler attack on Palestinians harvesting olives in the West Bank village of Abu Falah, Friday. Leo Correa/AP hide caption
Israeli police issued a statement acknowledging reports that a foreign journalist was injured and said it would investigate the incident and "bring those involved to justice."
The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attempted to cast some doubt on the story, asserting on social media that the facts "remain unclear and are under investigation." Murray, the Post's executive editor, quickly clarified. "To be clear: Some facts are neither in dispute nor unclear. Our photographer was clearly marked as Press. She was clearly beaten," he wrote in a quote post on X of the Israeli leader's statement.
The U.S. State Department said it was aware of the reports and that it contacted The Washington Post to offer consular assistance. "We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and support appropriate investigations as well as legal accountability for those responsible," the State Department said, without mentioning the assault of the American photojournalist.
Palestinian volunteers douse an olive tree set on fire along with a Palestinian-owned vehicle, reportedly by Israeli settlers, near the village of Turmus Ayya, north of the city of Ramallah, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, on Friday. Ahmad Gharabli/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
There were two dozen settler attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters Friday, leaving 20 people injured, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent Society.
The United Nations' humanitarian office for Gaza and the West Bank said settler attacks during the olive harvest season have killed one Palestinian and damaged more than 2,500 olive trees or saplings.
The attacks came as groups of Israeli settlers have stepped up their assaults on Palestinians in the West Bank. They also follow another assault earlier this month, when Israelis beat Agence France-Presse photojournalist Jaafar Ashtiyeh as he was covering settler violence against Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank.
Sara Qudah, who handles the Middle East for the Committee to Protect Journalists, said Levine's beating was not an isolated incident for journalists covering the West Bank olive harvest. "It's part of a disturbing pattern of violence and harassment against journalists regardless of their nationalities," she said.
She added that the attackers have no reason to fear consequences because Israeli authorities fail to do anything to stop the violence.
The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate also condemned the attack as an "assault on press freedom" and a violation of rules protecting journalists during conflicts.
Nuha Musleh contributed reporting from Ramallah, West Bank.

articles.title_orig: Brush fires trigger evacuations in Los Angeles, Orange counties amid Santa Ana winds across SoCal
articles.title_zh: Brush fires trigger evacuations in Los Angeles, Orange counties amid Santa Ana winds across SoCal
articles.content_orig:
The Bryson Fire burns in Malibu, Calif., on Oct. 15, 2026. The brush fire in the mountains west of Los Angeles prompted evacuation warnings from officials, as powerful Santa Ana winds risked spreading the blaze rapidly.
Southern California towns are on high alert as the first Santa Ana winds of the season have arrived, igniting multiple blazes across the region.
The red flag warning put out by the National Weather Service (NWS) Wednesday evening followed a relatively quiet wildfire season so far in California . Only 300,000 acres had burned since Jan. 1, compared to the over one million acres that fires have usually burned by mid-October.
Santa Ana winds blow in from the desert, typically between the months of September and May. The winds bring warmer temperatures and drier air to Southern California. They also greatly increase the risk of wildfires—warm winds coupled with summer drought can often make for a dangerous combination. The January 2025 fires that tore through the Pacific Palisades and Altadena were fueled by Santa Ana wind gusts that reached 100 m.p.h.
This week’s winds will not be as strong , according to NWS predictions. But that doesn’t mean the area is in the clear. The NWS warned that, if any fires ignite, “conditions are favorable for extreme fire behavior.”
The largest fire, named the Henderson fire, erupted Thursday afternoon around Camp Pendleton, a San Diego Marine Corps training base, and had burned through 1,404 acres by Friday morning. Two other fires have burned through 200 acres and 43 acres in Los Angeles county.
The NWS issued a red flag warning on Oct. 15 for the Los Angeles County San Gabriel Valley forecast zone that will stay in effect until Saturday evening. The most extreme conditions are expected in the Ventura and Los Angeles County valleys and mountains, particularly Santa Clarita, Thousand Oaks, and Simi Valley.
As of Thursday night, Southern California Edison shut off power to tens of thousands of customers. Nearly 90,000 PG&E customers were also left without power. Shutting down power helps stop downed power lines or aging infrastructure from sparking fires.
If you live in an impacted area, sign up for local emergency alerts, plan for power outages, and avoid any outdoor activities that might ignite sparks like BBQs, campfires, or discarded cigarette butts.
One Southern California town is even encouraging residents to secure hallowed decorations—the giant skeleton and inflatable pumpkins haunting front lawns. High winds can turn Halloween decorations into hazards,” the city of Pasadena said in a Facebook post. “Secure them before winds pick up.”

articles.title_orig: Women's rights taking big steps in China
articles.title_zh: Women's rights taking big steps in China
articles.content_orig:
After writing about the injustices women faced in ancient China, I began to wonder how much their rights and social status have changed in modern China.
A conversation with my friend Amy, a teacher who lives in Canada and had recently visited her family in Beijing, helped me gain a better understanding of the current situation.
One interesting difference she shared with me was China’s retirement system. Traditionally, men have retired at age 60, while women have generally been eligible to retire earlier: at age 50 for female blue-collar workers and 55 for women in managerial and technical positions. Many people I know in China enjoy their retirement because they continue to receive a monthly pension and other benefits.
Have you ever heard the famous quote, “Women hold up half the sky,” attributed to Mao Zedong, the former chairman of the Chinese Communist Party? The statement reflects the idea that women are essential to society and make significant contributions to the nation’s development.
Women account for approximately 49.1% of China’s population. Of the country’s roughly 1.405 billion people, about 688 million are female, compared with 717 million males. Women also play a substantial role in the workforce. According to a modeled estimate from the International Labour Organization, the labor force participation rate for Chinese women aged 15 and older is approximately 59.15%. These figures demonstrate that women are an important part of China’s social and economic life.
Education is another area in which women have made considerable progress. In 2024, female students accounted for 50.76% of higher education enrollment and 50.1% of graduate students. This has helped create opportunities for women to pursue professional careers and assume leadership roles.
My own experiences in China have given me an even greater appreciation for women’s achievements, particularly in education and leadership. When I visited Wuxi, China, in May 2025, I noticed that many school principals were women. In the Binhu school district, six of the 14 elementary schools had women principals, and there were also 27 women serving as assistant principals.
One friend who has particularly inspired me is Ms. Pan Wangji. When I first met her in 2005, she was the principal of Daoxiang Experimental Elementary School. She later advanced to become the chief of education bureau for the Binhu school district, an equivalent of a school district superintendent in the United States. Her career is an inspiring example of how women can advance into positions of significant responsibility and influence.
China has made significant progress in expanding women’s access to education, employment, and leadership opportunities. Gender equality has also been established as a basic national policy. Amy shared her view that women and minority groups receive support and protection at the leadership level.
Research on leadership has also offered encouraging insights into women’s leadership abilities. Studies and meta-analyses suggest that women often receive higher ratings in certain aspects of leadership effectiveness, particularly emotional intelligence and transformational leadership. Transformational leadership involves inspiring trust, motivating team members, and supporting individual growth and development.
In my previous article, I wrote about "Against the Current," an impressive historical drama directed by Huang Yingxiang, a young female filmmaker born in the 1990s. Working closely with the playwright, she uses storytelling to explore women’s experiences and struggles, bringing to the forefront perspectives that have not always received the attention they deserve. The work also creates a space for reflection on women’s choices, resilience, and determination.
One particularly meaningful quote from the protagonist, Shen, captures this message:
“One faint lamp may only illuminate a small area, but if I light one lamp and you light another, then even the faintest lights, when gathered together, can illuminate an entire street.”
I find this message deeply moving because it reflects what I have learned throughout my own life: individual acts of kindness, encouragement, and support may seem small, but together they can make a tremendous difference.
During my years living in Owensboro, Kentucky, I met so many wonderful women through First Presbyterian Church, the Sierra Club, the American Association of University Women(AAUW), and Daviess County schools. Women such as Helen Sears, Judy, Aloma, Vickie R., Linda Y., and many others became mentors, role models, and sources of encouragement. Their kindness and guidance helped me grow into the person I am today. Each of them, in her own way, helped light a lamp along my path.
Inspired by their influence, I have sought to pass that same encouragement on to other girls and women. I volunteered at Owensboro Girls’ Inc. while living in Owensboro and continued my involvement even after moving to California. I am also proud that I wrote a skit about the American women’s movement, giving students in California the opportunity to reenact key moments in history and understand the struggles and sacrifices women have endured in the fight for the right to vote.
I am deeply grateful to the women who have helped illuminate my path, and I hope to do the same for others. If each of us lights a lamp and inspires another woman to light hers, together we can create a brighter future for generations to come. After all, even the faintest lights, shining together, can illuminate an entire street!

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Faces Weekly Loss on Tech Stock Slump — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Faces Weekly Loss on Tech Stock Slump — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks slid on Friday as traders notched a mostly losing week amid a shift away from tech and artificial intelligence-related names as well as a rise in oil prices.
The S&P 500 lost 1.09% and ended at 7,659.44, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 2.14% to close at 26,140.03. Both indexes ended the session below their 50-day moving averages. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 175.28 points, or 0.34%, to 52,002.41. The sell-off sent the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) above 22 for the first time in four months .
Chipmakers were lower again. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) lost 3%, led by declines in Micron Technology , Advanced Micro Devices and Sandisk . Semiconductors have struggled this week amid jitters about competition from China . The SMH slid 10% week to date for its biggest weekly decline since April 2025.
Those declines, coupled with drops in other stocks linked to AI, dragged the S&P 500 to a losing week. The benchmark index fell about 2% this week, while the Nasdaq shed more than 4% for its worst week since June. The Dow, on the other hand, advanced 0.7% on the week.
Investors have also grown concerned that tech companies are borrowing too much for the AI buildout . Shares of neoclouds like CoreWeave , which has seen its total debt rise to more than $51 billion , were down nearly 12%, bringing the stock's week-to-date losses to 25%.
"The question is: Is this a systemic issue?" said Michael Rosen, Angeles' chief investment officer. "Obviously, increased debt issuance is something to observe and continue to watch and be concerned about if it continues to get to levels of excessiveness. But we're not remotely close to that right now."
Other areas of the market such as energy saw gains Friday, with stocks like Chevron helping to keep the Dow's losses in check. Oil prices moved higher amid rising tensions between the U.S. and Iran as well as between Russian and Ukraine. West Texas Intermediate crude futures increased 3.51% to settle at $101.41 per barrel, while Brent crude futures advanced 3.72% to $109.86.
Simultaneously, investors have been grappling with hotter-than-expected inflation data, which has been exacerbated by elevated energy prices in the wake of the U.S.-Iran war. Wholesale inflation this week saw its biggest gain since 2022 , while consumer inflation remained well above the Federal Reserve's target of 2%.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke at an IMF event in Bangkok overnight. And while he didn't comment on whether the Fed would raise rates before year-end, traders took that as a sign that the central bank will hold policy steady later this month. The CME Group's FedWatch tool points to an 82% chance the Fed keeps its overnight rate unchanged at its Oct. 27-28 meeting.
The three leading U.S. indexes ended Friday's session with losses.
The S&P 500 dropped 1.09% to finish at 7,659.44, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 2.14% to 26,140.03. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 175.28 points, or 0.34%, to 52,002.41.
As the market sell-off intensified Friday afternoon, the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) rose to levels it last closed at four months ago.
The VIX rose to 21.32, as of 3:10 p.m., rising more than 4.8 points on the session. It's on pace for its highest close since June 10, when it closed at 22.22.
Typically, when the VIX is above 20 that indicates greater fear in the market. The index last closed above that level on July 29 , when markets fell after the Federal Reserve kept interest rates steady at its meeting that month. The next day , stocks rose, and the day marked a bottom in a market where many AI-related stocks had been selling off in the previous month .
The Nasdaq Composite was down about 2.5% in afternoon trading on Friday, bringing its loss on the week to almost 5%.
With that move, the tech-heavy index on pace for its worst weekly performance since the week ended April 4, 2025, when the index recorded a roughly 10% drop.
Communication services and information technology led the S&P 500 lower on Friday.
The two sectors were down 2.7% and 2.4%, respectively, becoming the two biggest laggards among the 11 S&P 500 sectors. Consumer discretionary followed behind them, falling 1.5%.
However, a look beneath the surface showed that the S&P 500 — which was last down 1.3% — was more evenly split despite the losses at the index level. There were about 280 losers in the index and 222 gainers.
In total, five out of the 11 S&P 500 sectors were in positive territory, led by energy with its 2.1% gain and utilities with its rise of 1.2%.
— Sean Conlon and Sarah Min
U.S. crude oil prices rose sharply Friday as Iran escalated its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz this week and Ukraine vowed to keep striking Russian refineries.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures were up 2.9% to $100.78 per barrel. Brent crude, the international benchmark, was 3.3% higher at $109.37 per barrel. Read more .

Early in the "SaaSpocalypse" that roiled software companies this year, Manish Gupta, a portfolio manager at First Eagle Investments, added to Workday as he parsed through the wreckage for some bargains.
In recent months, that bet has paid off for the value investor. After falling about 40% in the first quarter of 2026, during which the enterprise software stock at various points was trading at not even three times revenue, the stock went on to surge more than 55% in the third. It's also outperforming this week, rising more than 2% amid a broader tech sell-off as investors exit for safer assets.
Gupta, who attended the company's analyst day this week, remains confident in Workday, which he said is trading at a discount to similar businesses in the private markets. Workday is a top 10 holding in the First Eagle Global Fund (SGENX) , which he co-manages and which had nearly $75 billion in total net assets as of Sept. 30.
"The price has moved up, but the business has also become better," Gupta said. "The 'SaaSpocalypse' has also turned around, but the stock's still attractive."

articles.title_orig: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
articles.title_zh: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV has been pictured celebrating Mass from hospital, in the first images of him released by the Vatican since he underwent lung surgery.
The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.
The images shared on Friday showed the Chicago-born Pope wearing a green robe while standing behind a makeshift altar on the tenth floor of the hospital.
Pope Leo "celebrated with the medical and nursing staff" and thanked workers for their service, the Vatican press office said.
Also on Friday, the Pope phoned Russian President Vladimir Putin from hospital to urge a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where access to food and water has been cut off for thousands .
"The fact that he accepted the call and spoke with the Pope may, I hope, be a sign that the Pope's request will indeed be carried out," said Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican's secretary of state.
Without mentioning a ceasefire, the Kremlin said: "The Vatican's intention to help create the conditions necessary to ensure the safety of the town's population and to organise vital supplies has been supported".
"It has been agreed to cooperate on this matter," it added.
The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Turk, made a similar plea to address what he described as a "desperate" situation in Oleshky.
The Pope's doctors said on Friday tests had shown "a steady improvement in his general condition" since his surgery.
His doctors said that a chest X-ray indicated "good recovery of the operated lung".
The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.
"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before he spent a "peaceful night" at the hospital.
Pope Leo first announced that he would be having the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
The Vatican has stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure.
Additional reporting by Joel Guinto

articles.title_orig: China’s tourists flock to experience a pretend typhoon as ‘dark tourism’ flourishes
articles.title_zh: China’s tourists flock to experience a pretend typhoon as ‘dark tourism’ flourishes
articles.content_orig:
The concept of ‘paying to suffer’ soars in popularity, with simulated disasters proving a modern twist on visiting sites of historic tragedies
W hen Leon Lv was looking for somewhere to travel last year, she turned to the Chinese social media app RedNote for ideas. The algorithm took her to videos of people struggling to survive typhoon-strength winds and flash floods.
“I never experienced a typhoon. I don’t know how it will feel and what will happen. I just have seen it on the news,” says the 28-year-old from Chongqing in south-west China . “So that’s why I want to go there to have a safe place to experience it and learn something.”
She travelled more than 1,300km to Hangzhou in the east, and joined a group of 20 to take part in a disaster simulation that featured a typhoon-fuelled flooding scenario.
Standing in a simulated flood, her mind momentarily went blank as hundreds of tonnes of water swept people off their feet, and carried them towards a safety barrier. As the surge hit, she forgot she was in a simulation. “One thing I learned is how to stay calm and protect myself during a flood. I learned how to use the right body position to stay safe,” she says. “No book and no school [can] teach me like that.”
Across Chinese social platforms phrases like “paying to suffer”, or “paying to buy fear” are trending online as part of a wave of interest in experiences known as “dark tourism”.
Lvxing Base, a company in Hangzhou offering simulated disaster experiences has gone viral. The founders spent 10 years making documentaries in some of the world’s most extreme environments.
At a 200,000 square metre facility, which opened in 2024, they simulate extreme weather conditions like typhoons and mudslides, giving participants the experience of what it would be like in a disaster.
“I don’t deny that many people come because they want excitement,” says general manager Wang Kuanghan. They want to see what this place is like, what a real typhoon and torrential rain feel like, and whether they themselves can withstand it. Most of our individual customers are between 20 and 30 years old.”
It plans to open five more centres across China within the next three years. It also plans to create earthquake and fire simulations.
The offering are not limited to private companies. At Beijing’s Haidian public safety museum, tourists experience simulated earthquakes, tsunamis and fires using a 4D theatre, equipped with moving platforms and sound effects. Last year the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou opened a five-storey centre to teach visitors how to respond to emergencies and disasters. Its earthquake simulator can recreate ground shaking equivalent to a 7.2 magnitude quake.
Extreme weather has become increasingly common in China. In 2025, China recorded its highest number of hot days since records began, and was hit by 10 typhoons, well above the long-term annual average. China’s ministry of emergencies reported that 67 million people were affected by such disasters across the country.
In 2024, local governments were instructed to promote immersive disaster education, instructing safety centres, museums and training bases to use simulations to teach people how to respond in a real crisis.
“The new generation of Chinese travellers want to experience a place rather than simply see famous attractions,” says Robert Li, director of the School of Hotel and Tourism Management at the Chinese University of Hong Kong.
But some travellers have found a way to blend the two approaches; rather than indulging in the white-knuckle ride of a simulated typhoon, they are travelling to real sites of death and destruction.
In May 2008 a magnitude 8.0 earthquake devastated towns in China’s Sichuan province, killing more than 70,000 people. Alice*, a 30-year-old writer from Sichuan walked around Beichuan, one of the affected towns, the ruins of which the government had preserved. Metal beams hold collapsed buildings in place for the public to visit. She saw the site where schools collapsed, crushing students inside.
In Yingxue close to the epicentre, a broken clock surrounded by the remains of a middle school is frozen at 2.28, the moment the earthquake struck.
“I felt scared because of the power of nature and how many children and students could not escape from it,” says Alice, who plans to start a Chinese language Substack account detailing her journeys into tragedy. “Everything was so broken. It became like a ghost town, because nobody lives in the old town any more.”
Alice believes dark tourism helps a country reconcile with its past, even if the government decides what can be remembered.
In recent years, tour guide Samantha Wang has seen an increase in Chinese tourists attending the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall. In 1937 the Japanese Imperial army captured Nanjing, and Chinese official accounts say 300,000 civilians and soldiers were killed over weeks of massacres. Japan’s official position is that it acknowledges that large numbers of civilians were killed but says the number of victims is “difficult to determine”.
Entry to the hall is free but tourists must book online The local government reserves 25,000 places a day. In August, tickets to attend the museum are frequently sold out in advance, she says.
“There are more tragic sites in China, and I see more people interested to know about that. That’s a new trend” says Wang.
Inside the memorial hall hang photos of victims. “They [visitors] feel sad when they see those pictures, when they see those kids who were killed … After the visit, they feel relieved, and they feel encouraged that they should work harder to make China stronger,” she says.
Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li in Taipei

articles.title_orig: Thunderbird at ASU ranked No. 1 in the world for international trade, 5 years in a row
articles.title_zh: Thunderbird at ASU ranked No. 1 in the world for international trade, 5 years in a row
articles.content_orig:
QS global ranking places Thunderbird ahead of INSEAD, Cambridge and Oxford
Thunderbird School of Global Management at Arizona State University, located in downtown Phoenix, was the only school to earn a perfect overall score of 100, placing first among nearly 110 universities and business schools worldwide offering graduate programs in international trade. Photo courtesy of Thunderbird School of Global Management
For the fifth consecutive year, Thunderbird School of Global Management at Arizona State University has been recognized as the world leader in international trade by Quacquarelli Symonds, the prestigious global authority on higher education rankings.
The 2027 QS International Trade Rankings for MBA and master’s programs once again position Thunderbird as the No. 1 school in the world. The school ranks ahead of the University of Miami, the University of Michigan — Ann Arbor (Ross) and Columbia University in the U.S., as well as INSEAD (France), the University of Cambridge and the University of Oxford internationally.
“To be recognized as the world’s No. 1 institution for international trade for a fifth consecutive year is an extraordinary honor that our faculty, students and alumni should take great pride in,” said Charla Griffy-Brown , director general and dean of Thunderbird. “Their scholarship, ambition and impact challenge us to keep redefining international trade education.”
“From our undergraduate programs to our master’s curriculum, Thunderbird brings global commerce, emerging technology and leadership together. We prepare students from around the world to open markets, navigate disruption and create opportunity across borders,” Griffy-Brown said.
Thunderbird was the only school to earn a perfect overall score of 100, placing first among nearly 110 universities and business schools worldwide offering graduate programs in international trade. It was one of only three institutions in the world to surpass 90 points, and finished well ahead of the next highest-ranked school, Durham University in the United Kingdom, which received a score of 92.7.
Thunderbird also remains the only institution from the United States, and the Americas, to rank among the global top 10, with the University of Miami appearing next at No. 13. The school held this distinction in both 2026 and 2025, following its recognition in 2024 as one of only five U.S. institutions to place in the top 10.
Thunderbird's world-class faculty are central to this recognition, earning the school a No. 6 global ranking in the "Faculty Industry Experience and Engagement" category. This distinction reflects their active engagement with leading academic and industry organizations Including the Academy of International Business, African Continental Free Trade Area–Industrial Development Council, Business Association for Latin American Studies, Council on Foreign Relations, United Nations Conference on Trade and Development–Train for Trade, United Nations Economic Commission for Europe and the World Economic Forum. .
Locally, faculty and students are engaged with the Arizona District Export Council, the Diplomatic Corps of Arizona, the Phoenix Council on Foreign Relations and other key regional organizations.
Thunderbird faculty are also regularly featured and cited in leading international outlets, contributing scholarship and policy insights that shape global discourse. Their work has informed the strategies of prominent global institutions and has been referenced Influential bodies such as the Academy of Management, CFA Institute, Decision Sciences Institute, INFORMS, United States International Trade Commission, the National Intelligence Council, the United States Senate and the Departments of State and Defense have drawn upon this research. at the highest levels of policymaking.
Developed in collaboration with the Hinrich Foundation, schools are evaluated across several key performance indicators, including trade program content, graduate outcomes, industry engagement, innovative teaching, reputation and research.
The QS rankings specifically highlight Thunderbird’s flagship Master of Global Management program as the premier graduate program in international trade.
“Thunderbird stands out for the breadth and depth of its trade-related curriculum and for program attributes that employers tell us are critical in preparing graduates for successful leadership careers in global trade,” said Alex Boome , program director at the Hinrich Foundation. “The Hinrich Foundation is proud to support that preparation by awarding three scholarships each year to outstanding incoming students in Thunderbird’s MGM program.”
Each of these three Global Trade Leader scholarships, announced in May of this year, provides $25,000 from the Hinrich Foundation, complemented by $18,000 from the Thunderbird Alumni Scholarship, with additional merit-based awards available. The scholarships are open to incoming applicants from all countries who have relevant work experience and a strong interest in a global trade career.
As part of the QS World University Rankings, the International Trade Rankings help prospective students identify degree programs that prepare them to excel in global trade, while offering universities a benchmark for strengthening the quality and impact of trade education worldwide.
“Equally impressive is what our students achieve as they emerge ready to take their place on the global stage,” Griffy-Brown said. “They graduate with more than business skills and acumen. They bring the global perspective, technological fluency and practical experience to navigate complexity, work across cultures and turn uncertainty into opportunity. In a global environment unlike any we have seen before, our graduates are career-ready, prepared to thrive and equipped to shape what comes next.”

articles.title_orig: Indonesia needs predictable rules to keep Chinese capital
articles.title_zh: Indonesia needs predictable rules to keep Chinese capital
articles.content_orig:
Peer reviewed analysis from world leading experts
Chinese investors in Indonesia’s nickel sector have complained of rising taxes, abrupt rule changes and opaque enforcement, and alleged extortion. Jakarta has eased some concerns case by case but left the underlying problems unresolved. Indonesia is right to seek a fair return from its resources and to enforce environmental laws, and sunk investment gives it leverage. But it needs predictable rules, published standards and working appeals to turn that leverage into local development without deterring the next round of Chinese investment.
An unusually blunt letter to Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto, reported in May 2026, laid out Chinese investors’ grievances around the challenges of doing business in Indonesia — from over-enforcement to extortion . Jakarta’s response has been more familiar. Ministers convene companies, adjust a few policies and leave the harder questions to be settled case by case. This may ease tensions, but does little to make Indonesia’s investment regime easier to navigate.
The letter, from the China Chamber of Commerce in Indonesia, described six main problems . Higher taxes, backed by more intensive inspections, had raised operating costs, while planned foreign exchange retention requirements would severely harm corporate liquidity. Lower nickel quotas, project suspensions, tighter forestry law enforcement and stricter work-visa scrutiny had disrupted existing plans.
The chamber criticised opaque enforcement of tax, forestry and environmental rules. It claimed that a higher benchmark price and revised pricing rules had increased nickel ore costs by 200 per cent, and warned of possible export duties, an end to electric-vehicle incentives and less tax relief for special economic zones. It also alleged extortion and blocked appeal channels, saying some disputes could be resolved only through costly intermediaries.
Jakarta did not ignore these concerns, though not every subsequent development can be credited to the letter. On 11 May 2026, two days before the letter was reported , the government postponed planned mining-royalty increases . After the letter emerged, three ministers met around 30 Chinese mining companies. New foreign exchange retention rules also granted flexibility to exporters from qualifying partner countries , which officials later said include China .
Jakarta’s response has so far been selective. The royalty postponement eased one concern and the retention provision may help eligible Chinese exporters, but the ministerial meeting produced no publicly reported resolution. Nickel production controls remain tight. A September revision to the benchmark-pricing formula lowered the reference price for low-grade nickel ore, partly addressing the pricing complaint. The government has announced no changes to appeal procedures, work-visa administration or enforcement standards, nor publicly resolved the hydropower and forestry disputes.
Earlier expansion benefited from political sponsorship and investment incentives . As Jakarta tightens regulation, firms that committed capital under earlier arrangements must navigate new obligations. The first China–Indonesia Comprehensive Strategic Dialogue in August 2026 provides a standing forum , but does not itself create predictable procedures for regulatory disputes. The question is how political support that secured investment translates into consistent administrative decisions once projects are operating.
Indonesia need not freeze its mining rules. Finite resources should deliver a fair public return, under-invoicing must be curbed and environmental laws enforced. There is also a case for managing nickel production , since excessive output can depress prices and accelerate reserve depletion. Jakarta’s challenge is to pursue these aims through rules firms can anticipate, rather than abrupt interventions followed by private negotiation.
Indonesia can act against individual companies , as 2025 sanctions in the Indonesia Morowali Industrial Park show. But inspections after breaches cannot compensate for weak routine monitoring, fragmented mandates and unclear appeals. Environmental assessments, emissions reporting and community-development obligations are already law, yet a review by the International Institute for Sustainable Development identifies gaps in enforcement and industrial-safety inspection .
Chinese firms are unevenly prepared for higher standards. Another study by the institute found some have created environmental, social and governance teams, adopted international audits and strengthened safety systems, but judged sector-wide management to be at an early stage, with weak community engagement and public disclosure. Formal systems do not guarantee better performance, particularly with contractors, so credible Indonesian oversight remains indispensable.
Jakarta still has room to demand more. The International Energy Agency estimates that Chinese companies account for around 75 per cent of Indonesia’s nickel-refining capacity . They cannot relocate these plants cheaply, though they can curtail operations. Their greater leverage lies in future expansion — they can redirect new projects and remain a major source of the capital and technical capability needed for more advanced processing.
Investment flows are not a proxy for confidence. Chinese investment reached US$2.2 billion in the first quarter of 2026, before the letter became public, and may partly reflect earlier commitments. Companies can keep financing existing projects while growing cautious about new ones.
The harder test is whether downstreaming produces local development . It has raised export earnings and regional output, but processing ore domestically does not automatically create Indonesian suppliers, technical skills or research capacity. Rigid localisation risks deterring investors capable of transferring knowledge.
According to Indonesia’s Investment Coordinating Board, the planned Sambalagi high-pressure acid leaching project will include local training, a research centre and collaboration with Indonesian universities . These are promising commitments, not proof of delivery, and project-level pledges cannot replace published, measurable expectations for skills development, local procurement and community participation.
Both tests require tying higher standards to ordinary administration. Jakarta should consult before changing major requirements and provide credible transition periods, while environmental agencies should publish baseline data and inspection results. Penalties should be accompanied by published reasons and a usable appeal process, and companies should disclose their labour and procurement outcomes.
Indonesia’s balancing act can be sustained only if greater public revenue helps build the regulatory and local capabilities that downstreaming requires. Sunk investments give Chinese firms reason to adjust to clearer environmental and social demands , while uniform enforcement and credible transition periods give future investors a basis for planning. If enforcement remains fragmented and concessions selective, Jakarta may secure more from existing projects, but at the cost of a more cautious next round of investment.
Muhammad Faiz Krisnadi is a policy researcher based in Singapore.

articles.title_orig: Live updates: Father and teacher hailed for preventing further tragedy in Bend, Oregon, school shooting
articles.title_zh: Live updates: Father and teacher hailed for preventing further tragedy in Bend, Oregon, school shooting
articles.content_orig:
Police say a 16-year-old former student carried out the attack that killed three children and a teacher in a special needs classroom.
• Community in mourning: Police say a 16-year-old gunman killed three children and a teacher Thursday at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon. Another child and teacher were hospitalized. All the victims were shot in one special needs classroom , police said.
• Heroic actions: A father of two students saw the gunman and followed him into the school, fatally shooting him to stop the attack, officials said. Police commended the man’s heroism and the actions of a teacher who tackled the shooter and fought to disarm him.
• What we know about the shooter: The teen previously attended special needs classes at Silver Rail, according to investigators. Authorities have searched the gunman’s home but a potential motive remains under investigation. “I’m so sorry,” the boy’s mother told CNN .
• Grim total: This is the 36th shooting on K-12 school grounds across the United States this year, according to a CNN data analysis.
A 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher are receiving treatment at local hospitals after being critically injured at the school shooting in Bend, Oregon, police said today.
The child, who has not been identified, had received first aid at the scene and is now in “serious but stable condition” at Oregon Health & Science University Hospital, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said at a news conference today.
The educational assistant in the special education department, identified as Becky Drury , suffered “serious but non-life-threatening injuries” and is being hospitalized at St. Charles Bend, Krantz said.
Three children and a teacher were killed in the shooting Thursday, according to authorities.
Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher who was killed in the Silver Rail Elementary School shooting yesterday, “loved those children” and being an educator, her family said in a statement.
“Her goal was to be an educator and teach in the school district she loved growing up in,” the family said in a statement read at a news conference today.
The family described her as a “compassionate” person with a “huge heart” who “always fought for the underdog and those with special needs.”
Lambert was an Oregon native who grew up in Bend, graduated from Mountain View High School in 2019 and from Boise State in 2023, her family said. She also traveled to Barcelona, Spain, for an English teacher training school. She was a substitute teacher at Silver Rail before becoming a full-time teacher there.
“She loved Silver Rail; this was her dream job,” the family said.
Lambert was passionate about sports and had been a volleyball coach, her family said. She turned down pay her first season as a coach to help families who couldn’t afford to participate.
Lambert’s family says she was “funny and opinionated, and she lit up the room.”
Police and school officials just gave an update on the latest information from their investigation into the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School, which left at least three kids and one teacher dead.
Big questions still remain, including any potential motive.
CNN’s Emma Tucker, Maria Aguilar Prieto, Andi Babineau, Dalia Faheid and John Miller contributed reporting.
The teenager who opened fire at Silver Rail Elementary School on Thursday, killing three students and a teacher inside a single classroom, has been identified as Griffin J. John II, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz announced at a news conference Friday.
The shooter used a Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun in the attack, Krantz said. The gun had been purchased by his mother, a senior law enforcement official briefed on the investigation told CNN earlier Friday.
He had about 44 remaining rounds of 12-gage ammunition, Krantz said.
The shooter had approached the campus, dropped the shotgun over a fence, then climbed over and forced his way into the building, opening fire inside the classroom, according to Krantz.
The shooter’s mother spoke to CNN off camera from her balcony, but would not comment on how her son got access to the weapon. Investigators say that is still under investigation.
“I miss my boy. I’m so sorry,” the woman said as she cried and smoked a cigarette.
And in a message to the families of those killed, she said, “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss.”
The shooter’s parents were interviewed on Thursday and were cooperative with investigators, the official told CNN earlier Friday. The teen had attended the elementary school, though no clear motive for the shooting has been uncovered, authorities said Friday.
The shooter was previously a special needs student at the school and the shooting occurred in the special needs classroom, Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said. During the pandemic, his mother spoke with CNN affiliate KTVZ about how she hopes the in-person classes for special needs kids will resume. The program is described as being for kids with “intensive behavioral and social skills challenges.”
CNN has reached out to the program for comment.
A search warrant was executed on the shooter’s home Thursday, with investigators recovering computers and other electronic devices. Additional warrants have been obtained to retrieve data from the devices, according to the source.
CNN’s Nick Watt and Norma Galeana contributed reporting.
The teacher who was shot and injured at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, yesterday has been identified as Becky Drury, 54, an educational assistant in the special education department, family spokesperson Zack Hall said.
“We are incredibly grateful for the outpouring of support, prayers, and well-wishes following yesterday’s tragedy at Silver Rail Elementary,” Drury’s husband, Will Drury, said in a statement.
The family asked for privacy and is declining interviews at this time, according to the statement and the family spokesperson.
“We ask that you continue to hold everyone affected by this tragedy in your thoughts,” the statement concluded.
It is not yet clear why the shooter was able to bypass security measures at Silver Rail Elementary School before the deadly shooting, the district’s superintendent said.
Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook told reporters he couldn’t say “with confidence” how the gunman got through the doors, but the district is going to do “a lot of reviewing of our procedures.”
All schools in the Bend-La Pine Schools district are equipped with “secure vestibules” at the entrance of each of its buildings and a classroom door locking system, according to the school district’s website .
But Chief Mike Krantz of the Bend Police Department said during today’s news conference that the shooter was able to breach the building by shooting multiple rounds into glass panes in an external set of double doors.
All of the victims who were shot at Silver Rail Elementary School on Thursday were inside a special needs classroom that included students of mixed ages, said Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook.
The shooter was also a former special needs student at the school, said Cook.
Officials could not confirm whether the shooter had been a student in that particular classroom in the school, said Sheila Miller, communications manager for the Bend Police Department.
Rhoam Summer, 5, has been identified by authorities as one of the children killed in the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School.
Authorities will not be releasing the identities of the other two child victims at the request of their families, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.
The motive behind the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School is still under investigation, including if there were any mental health concerns or warning signs, according to Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz.
“Everyone wants to know why, including us,” Krantz said, referring to a motive.

articles.title_zh: Gretchen Walsh Clocks 22.75 To Break Own 50 SCM Free World Record At UVA Pro Elite SCM Worlds Prep Meet

Leading from start to finish, Walsh clocked 22.75, taking 0.08 off the 22.83 she swam at the 2024 Short Course World Championships. Archive photo via Jack Spitser/ Spitser Photography
October 16th, 2026 International , National , Records
The third and final session of the UVA Pro Elite SCM Worlds Prep Meet opened with a bang, as Gretchen Walsh broke her own World Record in the women’s 50 SCM freestyle.
Leading from start to finish, the 23-year-old UVA pro clocked 22.75, lowering her own World Record of 22.83 from the 2024 Short Course World Championships by 0.08 and Kate Douglass ’ hours-old U.S. Open Record and former world-leading time of 22.94 by 0.19.
Walsh now owns the three fastest swims in history, which account for three of the five sub-23 swims ever.
Earlier in the meet, Walsh was runner-up to Virginia training partner Kate Douglass in the 100 free, clocking her second-fastest ever time of 50.32, before swimming 53.04 in the 100 fly this morning , the third-fastest swim in history behind her pair of 52-point swims from the 2024 SC Worlds.
Expect to see Walsh likely back in action at the Short Course World Championship Trials at the end of the month, where she will have the opportunity to book her spot on her second SC Worlds team. Her first, in 2024, was a historic success: she won seven gold medals in seven events and set 11 World Records (along with 14 American Records), surpassing Mark Spitz and Michael Phelps for the most all-time records broken at a single competition. For her efforts, not surprisingly, Walsh was named Swimmer of the Meet.

articles.title_orig: Oregon shooting victims: three boys and female teacher killed at elementary school
articles.title_zh: Oregon shooting victims: three boys and female teacher killed at elementary school
articles.content_orig:
Father of five-year-old Rhoam Summer says family ‘broken and lost’, while seven-year-old and 54-year-old in hospital
Authorities are investigating a shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon , where a 16-year-old shooter killed four people before being shot dead by a bystander.
The shooting took place on Thursday afternoon at Silver Rail elementary school, about 125 miles (200km) south-east of Portland.
Here is what we know so far about the four victims, including three children aged five, eight and 11, and a 25-year old teacher, as well as the two people injured.
In a Facebook group post, Rhoam Summer’s father Kelik Summer posted about his five-year old son’s death, saying that Thursday was “the worst day of my life.” He added: “My son Rhoam was killed in a school shooting. We are broken and lost, but are surrounded by friends and family who are keeping us safe.”
Rhoam’s grandfather Bryan Jolly also confirmed his grandson’s death to the New York Times. Jolly described the tragedy as “senseless and a shock”, adding that Rhoam was “in my house a lot and in my garden with me and wrestling with me on the couch”.
“He was very bright and very mischievous and very fun-loving, and totally without fear,” Jolly said.
A separate GoFundMe page that appears to have been set up by friends of Rhoam’s family said: “In the wake of an unimaginable tragedy, the Summer family is grieving the heartbreaking loss of their sweet five-year-old son, Rhoam. There are no words that can ease the pain of losing a child, and no family should ever have to experience a loss like this.”
Bend police also confirmed Rhoam’s identity on Friday afternoon.
Police are not releasing his identification at his family’s request.
Police are not releasing his identification at his family’s request.
Twenty-five-year old Megan Lambert, a teacher at the school, was identified as another victim killed in the shooting, Bend police said on Friday.
In a statement shared with Bend police, Lambert’s family said: “Megan was a native central Oregonian. She grew up in Bend. She had a passion for playing sports, especially volleyball. She was a volleyball coach. She actually turned down pay for her first season as a coach, so families who couldn’t afford to participate could have the chance to play the sport she loved.”
“Her goal was to be an educator, and teach in the school district she loved growing up in … Silver Rail was her first job as a teacher, though she subbed there for many years … She loved Silver Rail. This was her dream job. Megan was compassionate and had a huge heart,” her family added.
The Central Oregon Volleyball Club website lists Megan as a local high school coach and describes her as a “blessing” who has done “so much for her team”.
Seven-year old Saylor Graham was injured in the shooting, according to several GoFundMe accounts set up by co-workers and friends of her family. “The family is focused on being at the hospital while their child fights for their life,” one account said.
“Right now, they are carrying the impossible weight of traveling to and from the hospital, staying near their child, caring for their other child, trying to keep up their household, and missing work during this crisis,” it added.
A business partner of Saylor’s mother, Danielle Graham, declined to be interviewed but confirmed Saylor’s identity to the Guardian.
Meanwhile, Bend police said on Friday that a seven-year old girl who was shot “is receiving life-saving care” at Oregon Health & Science University hospital in Portland, adding: “She is in serious but stable condition.”
Fifty-four-year old Becky Drury was also injured in the shooting, with her mother-in-law Yvonne Drury posting on Facebook: “Our wonderful daughter-in-law, Becky was shot thr[ough] her left arm and right hand, and is recovering in the hospital after surgery this afternoon.”
In the same post, Becky’s son Will Drury said: “Her left arm took a lot of damage so there’s a long recovery and more surgeries ahead. Her right hand took a hit as well, which also required surgery, but it is much less severe. The good news is she will be OK and we all get to keep that magnificent woman we love so much in our lives.”
Bend police said on Friday: “The injured 54-year-old female teacher suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries and is currently receiving treatment at St Charles Bend [hospital].”

articles.title_orig: How China Has Quietly Taken a Lead in International Agency Staffing
articles.title_zh: How China Has Quietly Taken a Lead in International Agency Staffing
articles.content_orig:
The front of the World Health Organization building in Geneva, Switzerland, on December 3, 2019. China has sought to staff the middle ranks of the international civil service, write Mike  Kuiken and Leland Miller. (Shutterstock/Diego Grandi)
Since 2020, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission has published a ledger of Chinese citizens holding senior positions across the international system, agency by agency, and the April 2026 edition lists five at the International Seabed Authority (ISA), an institution few Americans have even heard of. Under the World Health Organization ( WHO ), which everyone has heard of, it lists none.
Earlier this month, Beijing nominated Song Li, a National Health Commission official who has spent years on WHO technical committees, for the post of WHO director-general. This leadership contest is only one part of China ’s effort to shape international institutions. Across international institutions, Beijing is seeking to fill middle- and senior-level posts where officials (whose tenures often outlast leadership terms) draft standards, interpret procedures, process applications, and shape the choices that reach leadership for approval. Washington counts Beijing’s people at the top. The more consequential question is who holds the pen underneath.
In Kingston, Jamaica, the official who runs the office that processes applications to mine the deep ocean floor is Yongsheng Cai , a former Chinese foreign ministry official. He sits at the International Seabed Authority , which regulates mining on the half of the planet’s seabed that lies beyond any nation’s jurisdiction, and applications to explore and eventually extract the metals that go into electric-vehicle batteries cross his desk before they reach anyone else. He is one of five Beijing-aligned appointees in senior staff and oversight posts at the authority, and none of them arrived there by accident.
For years Washington has measured Chinese influence by the top jobs, and by that measure Beijing peaked in 2020 , when Chinese officials ran four United Nations agencies at once: food and agriculture, telecommunications, civil aviation, and industrial development. By 2023 , they had left three of those four top jobs, with only Qu Dongyu winning a second term at the Food and Agriculture Organization. Beijing’s candidate also lost the 2020 race for the World Intellectual Property Organization leadership. At Interpol, China’s candidate, Meng Hongwei, won the presidency in 2016; Beijing summoned him home two years later and imprisoned him (his resignation letter arrived from custody).
That run of departures may seem like proof that Beijing is in retreat. But it obscures an influence strategy that has been underway beneath the agency heads. Beijing’s influence in that layer persists through leadership changes, even as its WHO bid signals renewed ambition for the top jobs—just when Washington has walked away from the table.
Plenty of serious people in Washington, in both parties, regard these institutions as sluggish, politically captured, and venues for anti-American speeches. They are not wrong. However, the institutions exist anyway, and they decide who mines the seabed, who gets which radio frequencies, and how international trademark-registration systems operate, whether or not the United States is in the room. Every American city has a zoning board that will rule on the building next door whether or not you show up, and the people who do show up write the rules.
In intellectual property, Binying Wang , the Chinese nominee who lost the 2020 contest for Director General of the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), remained deputy director general for its brands and designs sector for years afterward. WIPO’s current leadership listing identifies her successor as Shen Changyu , who ran China’s patent and trademark office for 12 years. The individual has changed; Chinese representation in the portfolio that administers the international trademark and design-registration systems has continued.
In civilian technology, the Standardization Administration of China serves as the secretariat for 95 Technical Committees and subcommittees of the International Organization for Standardization, including the one drafting global standards for brain-computer interfaces. These systems connect brain activity to computers. Technical standards bodies may sound obscure, but the point is simple: standards built around a country’s existing technologies can give its companies a head start, leaving competitors to adapt their products.
The International Telecommunication Union ( ITU ) coordinates international use of the electromagnetic spectrum, the radio waves that carry everything from cell signals to satellite internet, and the Commission’s April 2026 ledger lists no Chinese citizen in its General Secretariat, which again looks like a retreat until you check the layer below. Witnesses at the Commission’s April 2025 hearing on China’s space program cited Chinese filings covering more than 74,000 low-earth-orbit satellites. Every one of those filings has to clear the union’s coordination rules, which are written by consensus at its conferences and interpreted by a twelve-member board, so whoever controls the room and the board controls the orbits. They described Beijing’s practice of flooding union and World Radiocommunication Conference sessions with enough personnel to overwhelm consensus.
For the telecommunications union’s elections in Doha this November, Beijing has nominated Cheng Jianjun , an executive vice president of China Mobile, for another term on the 12-member Radio Regulations Board , which interprets the Radio Regulations and handles associated disputes. A government able to send more people than anyone else to handle problems such as these does not especially need the secretary-general’s office.
The private sector needs the tools to defend itself from unconventional drone or cyber threats.
Foreign and malign actors constantly exploit weak ownership reporting requirements to launder money throughout the United States.
The frozen conflict in Cyprus is a major roadblock to integrating one of NATO’s most powerful militaries into European defense initiatives.
The International Monetary Fund’s ( IMF ) general counsel is Yan Liu , a Chinese citizen. Her department helps shape the IMF’s sovereign debt policies and supports the Common Framework and the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable , processes where China’s role as a major creditor is consequential. China is the largest bilateral lender to the developing world and has a well-documented record of lending on secret terms in Zambia, Sri Lanka, and across the countries that have joined the Belt and Road Initiative . When those debts come up for restructuring, her office writes the IMF’s positions, a proximity to the referee no other creditor would be allowed.
A recent Center for Global Development study found that China’s formal voting power in these institutions still lags compared to the size of its economy, which is true. Yet that’s beside the point, because Beijing’s strategy isn’t to outvote anyone so much as staff the offices that write the rules the votes are about.
Congress rightly saw this problem coming years ago and wrote remedies into the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 , including a binding duty for the National Institute of Standards and Technology ( NIST ) to coordinate American participation in international standards bodies, and a pilot grant program to pay for the people who would do it. Congress gave the duty to NIST because setting standards is what NIST exists to do, and has done for the United States and much of the world since Congress created it in 1901.
Four years on, Congress should ask what that mandate has delivered: how many American experts are participating, which committees they lead, and where gaps remain. NIST announced a $15 million, five-year cooperative agreement with ASTM International in O

articles.title_orig: Oregon school shooter identified as 16-year-old whose mother purchased the gun he used, sources say
articles.title_zh: Oregon school shooter identified as 16-year-old whose mother purchased the gun he used, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Oregon school shooting: Police name victims and say suspect was former student
An Oregon teacher threw her mobile phone before she tackled and tried to wrestle away a shotgun from the arms of a teen suspect who opened fire on a special educational needs class.
As she tussled with him on the floor of the class - where three children and a teacher were killed - a bystander ran inside. Armed with a .40-caliber pistol, he opened fire and killed the teen.
The bystander, a dad of two girls at the school, had been driving past Silver Rail Elementary in Bend when he saw the suspect firing in the car park then shooting through a window to enter.
The details of the Thursday attack were confirmed by police, who said the 16-year-old suspect was a prior student at the school.
Police say the suspect was armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class.
"To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence, and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said on Friday.
Police offered more information on the attack at at a news conference on Friday, where they identified two of the four victims. They include five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.
The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said.
Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition.
Krantz said the heroic actions of both the teacher and the father who ran inside the school saved lives.
He said the teacher who wrestled with the gunman was not hurt but "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".
He identified the suspect as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, who previously attended the school and was a special educational needs student there.
A search warrant has been executed at the suspect's home and a search is ongoing, the police chief said.
Police believe the suspect travelled to the elementary school on foot, but police are still investigating his exact movements and how he acquired the gun. A motive is also not clear.
Police identified two of the victims as five-year-old Rhoam Summer (left) and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert (right)
Officials did not confirm the name of the father who intervened and fatally shot the suspect.
But Kaylub Giamanco's family has identified him to US media as the person who sprang into action.
The 36-year-old carpenter had just finished lunch and was on his way home when he passed the school, his brother told NBC News. He saw the suspect open fire on a vehicle outside the school then shoot through a window and go inside.
Police said he had a legally concealed .40 caliber in his vehicle and his brother said he grabbed the pistol "and decided to go in after" the suspect. Police say he fired at the suspect "multiple times", killing him.
In a statement to the BBC's partner CBS News, Giamanco's family said he is a "lifelong resident of Bend" and that he "is not seeking recognition".
The family said Giamanco wants to express his "gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support". He and his family "respectfully ask for privacy".
US President Donald Trump praised the bystander's actions on Friday, calling him a "great hero".
Addressing reporters at the White House before departing for Georgia, Trump said the situation could have been "much worse" with no intervention.
"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he said.
Without naming the bystander, Governor Kotek acknowledged the man's heroic actions stopping further loss of life, but noted they "carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well".
Kayla Epstein contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Archaeologists in Turkey may have found the world’s oldest shipwreck
articles.title_zh: Archaeologists in Turkey may have found the world’s oldest shipwreck
articles.content_orig:
The excavations have uncovered approximately 4,700-year-old amphorae believed to belong to what is described as the world's oldest known shipwreck. (Turkish Ministry of Culture and Tourism/Handout/Anadolu / Getty Images)
Archaeologists in Turkey have discovered what may be the world ’s oldest known shipwreck, with artifacts dating back nearly 5,000 years.
PAN AMERICAN PLANE FOUND 2,000 FEET UNDER ATLANTIC OCEAN AFTER CRASH 74 YEARS AGO
Although the ship itself has deteriorated, archaeologists uncovered ancient ceramic storage jars known as amphorae near Kekova Island, off Turkey's southern coast.
The jars date back approximately 4,700 years to the Early Bronze Age and are believed to have been used to transport goods across the Mediterranean .
ANCIENT SECRETS UNLOCKED OF HIDDEN UNDERGROUND FROM EXCEPTIONALLY PRESERVED SNAKE FOSSIL WITH SKULL INTACT
According to Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, Turkey's minister of culture and tourism, underwater excavations were conducted to shed light on the history of maritime trade along the Anatolian coast.
A diver handles a container during underwater archaeological excavations near Kekova Island in Antalya, Turkiye, on Oct. 14, 2026. ( Turkish Ministry of Culture and Tourism/Handout/Anadolu / Getty Images)
The ancient jars were discovered approximately 100 feet below the water’s surface, offering new insights into early trade connections across the eastern Mediterranean .
Clay analyses indicate that the amphorae were likely produced in workshops in the Jordan Valley. Similar examples have been found in Egypt, Troy and Crete.
MAN DISCOVERS MYSTERIOUS STONE OUTSIDE HOME, LEADING TO MASSIVE 3,300-YEAR-OLD EGYPTIAN TREASURE
An archaeologist discovered ancient ceramic storage jars. (Turkish Ministry of Culture and Tourism/Handout/Anadolu / Getty Images)
Researchers believe the amphorae were used to transport products such as olive oil or wine, suggesting the ship may have carried these goods across the Mediterranean.
Additionally, one of the amphorae discovered at the site featured nine different markings and two holes in its body.
ANCIENT 'LOST WORLD' COULD REWRITE HISTORY FOR HOW FIRST AMERICANS ARRIVED 13,000 YEARS AGO
Researchers believe the jar may have been used to churn cheese or butter, leading them to suggest that sailors produced their own food during long voyages.

articles.title_orig: On World Food Day, We Must Take Real Action on Global Malnutrition Crises
articles.title_zh: On World Food Day, We Must Take Real Action on Global Malnutrition Crises
articles.content_orig:
Save the Children Renews Call for Global Food Security Strategy
FAIRFIELD, Conn. (Oct. 16, 2026) — This World Food Day, Save the Children is calling for renewed action to ensure every child has access to the food and nutrition they need to survive, learn and thrive. Whether they face acute malnutrition in a humanitarian crisis or rely on nutrition programs here in the United States, children need consistent access to healthy food to reach their full potential.
As more than 43 million children across the globe suffer from severe malnutrition, [1] Save Children is also reiterating its call for the U. S. government to release its overdue Global Food Security Strategy.
The Global Food Security Act requires a new Global Food Security Strategy every four years. The strategy due in 2026 is yet to be released. At a time when hunger is worsening in many parts of the world and a “Super” El Niño is expected to worsen hunger and malnutrition in many parts of the world, the strategy can help guide U.S. efforts to identify emerging crises and support early and effective action – before children face serious health complications.
In an op-ed published by The Hill earlier this month, Save the Children President and CEO Janti Soeripto wrote : “The new Global Food Security Strategy should be built on a clear picture of where hunger is worsening, who is most vulnerable and which interventions stop a crisis before it becomes a catastrophe. It should treat early warning, early financing and early action as inseparable, strengthening tools like the Famine Early Warning Systems Network with better technology, nutrition data and information from frontline workers and communities.”
This year’s El Niño weather event – predicted to be one of the strongest in decades – is expected to deepen hunger and malnutrition further, because of dangerous droughts, crop failures, flooding and livestock losses.
Children in Somalia, Yemen and other countries facing conflict, extreme weather and economic instability need urgent support to prevent hunger from becoming a catastrophe.
World Food Day is also a reminder that child hunger remains a challenge in the United States . Federal nutrition programs, including the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), Child and Adult Care Food Program and school meals, help millions of children access healthy food and support their learning and development. Children cannot reach their full potential when they are hungry.
While acute malnutrition is both treatable and preventable, prevention requires sustained investment in nutrition, health systems, resilient food systems and early action before crises escalate.
Save the Children supports policies that reduce child hunger, improve nutrition and strengthen food security for children and families in the U.S. and around the world. Investing in children’s nutrition is one of the most effective ways to improve health, education outcomes and long-term opportunity.
In its programmatic work, Save the Children takes a comprehensive approach, investing in prevention, treating malnutrition and strengthening health systems while delivering food to children in need.
This World Food Day, Save the Children urges policymakers to prioritize actions that prevent hunger, protect children’s nutrition and help to build a future in which every child has the opportunity to grow up healthy and thrive.
[1] Levels and Trends in Child Malnutrition. Joint Child Malnutrition Estimates: Key findings of the 2025 edition; May 2025. UNICEF/WHO/World Bank Group/JME-Brochure-UNSDG-regions-2025-v23.pdf
Save the Children believes every child deserves a future. Since our founding more than 100 years ago, we've been advocating for the rights of children worldwide. In the United States and around the world , we give children a healthy start in life, the opportunity to learn and protection from harm. We do whatever it takes for children – every day and in times of crisis – transforming the future we share. Our results , financial statements and charity ratings reaffirm that Save the Children is a charity you can trust. Follow us on Facebook , Instagram , LinkedIn , X and YouTube .
